items.prompt: Git has checkout, revert, and reset, often used interchangeably in speech as “undo.” What actually distinguishes them?
choices: Nothing meaningful — they're interchangeable and any one works for any undo

checkout moves your working position (HEAD, or restores named files); revert adds a new commit that cancels an old one; reset moves the branch pointer, optionally touching staging and the working directory too
checkout and reset are identical; revert is just an older, deprecated name for both
revert only works on branches, checkout only works on files, reset only works on commits
items.explanation: The three commands genuinely target different things: checkout changes where you're standing (or restores specific files) without touching history; revert adds new history that cancels old history; reset moves what a branch points to, and can optionally overwrite staging and working-directory content too.
items.reference:
🔀 checkout — move HEAD, or restore files
⏪ revert — new commit, history untouched
⚠️ reset — moves branch pointer, optionally rewrites working dir

Why: each verb targets a genuinely different thing — history, a pointer, or the working directory.

items.prompt: Which of the three commands (checkout, revert, reset) is the only one that can add a brand-new commit to history rather than moving something backward?
choices: checkout
revert — it creates a new commit whose diff is the inverse of an old one; it never moves a pointer backward
reset
All three add new commits
items.explanation: revert is the odd one out: instead of moving a pointer or your working position, it computes the inverse of a past commit's change and commits that inverse as a brand-new commit, leaving every prior commit exactly where it was.

Why: each verb targets a genuinely different thing — history, a pointer, or the working directory.

items.prompt: What's the key difference between what git reset and git revert actually do to history?
choices: They're functionally identical; revert is just an older name for reset
reset moves the branch pointer backward (rewriting what the branch points to); revert adds a NEW commit that cancels out an old one, leaving history untouched and append-only
reset only works on files, revert only works on entire commits
revert deletes commits from the repository entirely; reset only hides them
items.explanation: This is the central distinction: reset rewrites what history a branch points to; revert never removes or rewrites anything — it adds a new commit whose effect is the inverse of an old one, keeping history append-only.
items.reference:
Rewrite: moves what already happened — risky once shared
Append: adds something new — safe even when shared
items.learnMore:
Rewriting history vs. appending to it

The same underlying question — “does anyone else already have a copy of what I'm changing” — decides which is safe.

CommandRewrite or append?Risk when shared
resetRewriteRisky once shared — orphans commits others have
revertAppendSafe always — nothing prior is touched

Common mistake

Assuming any command that changes what a branch “looks like” is equally risky. The risk isn't about how different the result looks — it's about whether anyone else already has a copy of what's being replaced.

items.prompt: Why does the rewrite-vs-append distinction matter “enormously,” in this unit's words, once more than one person shares a branch?
choices: It doesn't actually matter once a branch is shared — both are equally safe

Rewriting history that others already pulled leaves their copy referring to commits the remote no longer has, causing a divergent-history conflict on their next sync; appending never has that problem, since nothing anyone already has gets changed
Appending is always slower over a network than rewriting
It only matters if the team uses GitHub specifically
items.explanation: A rewrite invalidates any copy of the old history someone else already has — their next pull or push runs into commits the remote no longer recognizes. An append never has this problem because nothing that existed before is touched, only added to.

items.prompt: This unit calls checkout “the most overloaded of the three verbs.” What does that mean concretely?
choices: checkout is simply slower to run than the other two commands

Depending on what argument follows it (a branch name, a commit hash, or a file path), checkout can switch branches, detach HEAD to an old commit, or restore individual files — three different-shaped operations under one command name
checkout requires more typing than reset or revert
checkout is deprecated and should never be used
items.explanation: checkout historically covers three genuinely different operations depending on its argument's shape — branch switch, detached-HEAD move, or file restore — and conflating them under one verb is a real, common source of confusion, which is exactly what git's modern switch/restore split addresses.
items.reference:
🌿 A branch name → switches branches
📍 A commit hash → detached HEAD
📄 -- <file> → restores that file only

Why: one verb, three shapes of argument, three different behaviors.
items.learnMore:
checkout's overloaded meanings

Git 2.23 split checkout into switch (branches/commits) and restore (files) for exactly this reason.

ArgumentEffectModern split-out command
Branch nameMove HEAD + working dir to that branchgit switch
Commit hashMove HEAD there, detachedgit switch --detach
-- <file>Restore just that file's contentgit restore

Common mistake

Typing a bare `checkout .` or `checkout <path>` expecting it to behave like a narrow, single-file operation, when a bare directory path with no `--` restores everything underneath it.

items.prompt: Modern git offers `switch` and `restore` as alternatives to `checkout`. What problem were they introduced to solve?
choices: They're faster implementations of the exact same single behavior
They split checkout's overloaded behavior into two separate, unambiguous commands — switch for branches/commits, restore for files — so the argument's shape can't silently change what operation runs
They add support for remote repositories that checkout couldn't reach
They were introduced purely for backward compatibility with older git versions
items.explanation: switch and restore exist specifically to remove checkout's ambiguity: switch only ever moves HEAD (branches or commits), restore only ever touches file contents — neither can be confused with the other the way a single overloaded checkout invocation can.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Per L2, after `git reset` moves a branch pointer backward, what actually happens to the commits that used to be ahead of the new position?

They're moved to a separate “trash” branch automatically

items.explanation: reset doesn't delete anything outright — it just stops the branch from pointing at those commits. They linger in git's object store, invisible to normal history-walking commands, until eventually garbage collected, which is the window reflog-based recovery relies on.

Unreachable commits stay in the object store until garbage collected
